name: Quadrilaterals & Polygons
intro: **Classify the shape before writing a formula.** Most errors here are applying a rhombus fact to a parallelogram, or a cyclic fact to a general quadrilateral (§1).
For anything asking for the number of sides, start from the exterior angle 360/n — it is several times faster than the interior-angle formula (§5).

qs.q: A quadrilateral circumscribes a circle. Three consecutive sides measure 6, 8 and 9. Find the fourth side.
qs.h: §4 — in a tangential quadrilateral, the two pairs of opposite sides have equal sums.

qs.q: The area of a rhombus with diagonals 24 and 10 is
qs.h: §2 — half the product of the diagonals. Forgetting the half is the planted error.

qs.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 12 and 20 and height 9. Find its area.
qs.h: §3 — ½ (sum of the parallel sides) × height.

qs.q: Find the number of diagonals of a decagon.
The interior angle of a regular polygon is 156°. The number of sides is
qs.h: §5 — go via the exterior angle, which is always 360/n. Much faster than the interior-angle formula.

qs.q: The sum of the interior angles of a polygon is 1440°. Find the number of sides.
A regular hexagon of side 6 has area
qs.h: §6 — six equilateral triangles of side 6, or (3√3/2)a².

qs.q: A polygon has 54 diagonals. Find the number of sides.
qs.h: §5 — solve n(n − 3)/2 = 54, or just test the options mentally.

qs.q: A rectangle has perimeter 40. Find its maximum possible area.
qs.h: §7 — for a fixed perimeter, the square maximises the area.

qs.q: A rectangular field of area 400 m² is to be fenced. The least length of fence needed is
qs.h: §7 — the dual statement: for a fixed area, the square minimises the perimeter.

qs.q: A rectangular plot is fenced on three sides only (a wall forms the fourth) using 60 m of fencing. Find the maximum area (in m²).
qs.h: §7, the wall variant — the square is no longer optimal. Write A = x(60 − 2x) and use the vertex.
qs.s: 2x + y = 60 ⟹ A = x(60 − 2x), maximal at x = 15 ⟹ y = 30 ⟹ A = 450 m². (The square 15 × 15 would give only 225.)

audit: forgetting the equal-sums property of a tangential quadrilateral, a + c = b + d (§4)
dropping the ½ in the rhombus or trapezium area formula (§2, §3)
assuming the square is optimal even when one side is free — the wall variant has a 2 : 1 shape (§7)
using the interior-angle formula where the exterior angle 360/n is far quicker (§5)
misremembering the diagonal count as n(n − 1)/2, which counts all the sides too (§5)
recalling the hexagon area formula instead of splitting it into six equilateral triangles (§6)
confusing a square's side with its diagonal — area is ½d² (§2)
